n: Samuel serves under Eli at a time when revelation from God was rare. With corrupt priests at Shiloh, the heavens seemed mostly silent — much like the spiritual darkness before the Restoration.
Eli, old and nearly blind, has gone to bed. His failing eyesight may also hint at his spiritual dullness.
It is night, before the sanctuary lamp burned out toward dawn. Samuel is sleeping near the ark. God's lamp was still burning — hope had not gone out in Israel.

f.g: The golden lampstand, tended so it burned from evening to morning.

n: The Lord calls Samuel by name, and the boy answers, “Here am I” — the response of ready servants like Abraham, Moses, and Isaiah.
Samuel assumes Eli is calling and runs to him. Eli says he didn't call and sends him back to bed. Samuel's quick obedience shows his willing heart.
It happens a second time. Eli kindly calls him “my son” and again sends him back to bed.
The narrator explains: Samuel did not yet recognize the Lord's voice because he had not yet received revelation. Learning to recognize God's voice takes experience.

f.w: did not yet know the LORD

n: After the third call, Eli finally realizes the Lord is calling the boy. For all his failures, Eli still recognizes the things of God.
Eli teaches Samuel how to respond: “Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.” This becomes a model of humble willingness to listen and obey.

f.w: Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth

n: The Lord comes and stands there, calling “Samuel, Samuel.” Repeating a name shows tender, personal attention. Samuel answers as Eli taught him.

f.g: God's presence is described as personal and near.

n: The Lord's first message to young Samuel is a heavy one: He will do something in Israel so shocking it will make the ears of all who hear it ring.
God will fully carry out everything He warned about Eli's family. What He begins, He will finish.

f.w: all things which I have spoken

n: The reason is stated plainly: Eli knew his sons were blaspheming and degrading themselves, yet he did not restrain them. Parents and leaders are accountable for what they allow.

f.g: The Hebrew may also mean they “cursed God” — brought contempt on Him.

n: God has sworn that this sin will not be removed by sacrifice. Ritual offerings cannot cover deliberate, unrepented rebellion against God.
In the morning Samuel opens the sanctuary doors as usual, but he is afraid to tell Eli what God revealed. Delivering hard truth to someone you love is difficult.
Eli calls Samuel, using the tender words “my son,” and Samuel answers as he had to the Lord: “Here am I.”
Eli insists that Samuel tell him everything, even putting him under a solemn oath not to hide anything.

f.w: God do so to thee, and more also
f.g: an oath formula: may God punish you if you do not tell me

n: Samuel tells him everything. Eli accepts the judgment with resignation: the Lord is God and will do what is right. His submission is admirable, though he still does not act.

f.w: let him do what seemeth him good

n: Samuel grows up with the Lord beside him. God lets none of Samuel's prophetic words “fall to the ground” — everything he says by inspiration comes true.

f.w: did let none of his words fall to the ground

n: All Israel, from Dan in the far north to Beer-sheba in the far south, recognizes Samuel as a true prophet of the Lord.

f.g: A phrase meaning “the whole land” — from its northern to southern border.

n: Revelation returns to Shiloh. The silence of verse 1 has ended because God has a prophet again through whom He reveals His word.

f.w: the LORD revealed himself to Samuel
